questions.topic: Generalized Symmetric Randomized Facility Location Boundary Theorem
questions.prompt: Consider two agents on the real line $\mathbb{R}$ with true locations $x_1 \le x_2$ and distance $d = x_2 - x_1 > 0$. Consider the family of symmetric 3-point randomized mechanisms $f_p$ parameterized by $p \in (0, 1/2)$: $$f_p(x) = \begin{cases} x_1 & \text{with probability } p \\ x_2 & \text{with probability } p \\ \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2} & \text{with probability } 1 - 2p \end{cases}$$ *(Context: In Assignment 3 Q1e you studied $p = 1/6$; in Week 3 Lecture you studied $p = 1/4$.)* (a) (5 Marks) Prove that $f_p$ is strategyproof in expectation if and only if $p \ge 1/4$. Specifically: prove that if $p < 1/4$, an agent can strictly reduce her expected cost by misreporting outward; and prove that if $p \ge 1/4$, no unilateral misreport can strictly decrease her expected cost. (b) (3 Marks) Prove that among all strategyproof mechanisms in this family ($p \in [1/4, 1/2]$), the worst-case maximum-cost approximation ratio is exactly $\text{Ratio}(p) = 2p + 1$, and conclude that $p = 1/4$ is the unique optimal strategyproof mechanism achieving the lower bound ratio of $3/2$.
questions.blueprint:
Proof Blueprint (Exact Assignment Style)

Part (a): Strategyproofness Boundary ($p \ge 1/4$)

Step 1: Truthful Expected Cost
Let $x_1 \le x_2$ and $d = x_2 - x_1 > 0$. Under truthful reporting: - With probability $p$, the facility is at $x_1$: Agent 1's cost is $|x_1 - x_1| = 0$. - With probability $p$, the facility is at $x_2$: Agent 1's cost is $|x_2 - x_1| = d$. - With probability $1 - 2p$, the facility is at $\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$: Agent 1's cost is $\frac{d}{2}$. Agent 1's expected cost under truthful reporting is: $$\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}_1(\text{truth})] = p(0) + p(d) + (1 - 2p)\frac{d}{2} = \left( p + \frac{1 - 2p}{2} \right) d = \frac{d}{2}$$ Notice that this truthful expected cost is identically $\frac{d}{2}$ for ALL $p \in (0, 1/2)$!

Step 2: Analysis of Outward Deviation ($x_1' = x_1 - \delta$ with $\delta > 0$)
Suppose Agent 1 reports $x_1' = x_1 - \delta < x_1$. The reported positions are $x_1'$ and $x_2$. The new midpoint is $\frac{x_1' + x_2}{2} = \frac{x_1 - \delta + x_2}{2} = x_1 + \frac{d - \delta}{2}$. For any small $\delta \in (0, d)$, Agent 1's true distances to the three possible facility locations are: - At $x_1'$: distance is $|x_1 - (x_1 - \delta)| = \delta$. - At $x_2$: distance is $d$. - At midpoint: distance is $\left| \left( x_1 + \frac{d - \delta}{2} \right) - x_1 \right| = \frac{d - \delta}{2}$. Agent 1's new expected cost is: $$\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}_1(x_1')] = p(\delta) + p(d) + (1 - 2p)\left( \frac{d - \delta}{2} \right)$$ $$= p\delta + pd + \frac{1 - 2p}{2}d - \frac{1 - 2p}{2}\delta = \frac{d}{2} + \delta \left( p - \frac{1 - 2p}{2} \right) = \frac{d}{2} + \delta \left( 2p - \frac{1}{2} \right)$$ Examining the coefficient of $\delta$: $$\Delta \mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}_1] = \delta \left( 2p - \frac{1}{2} \right)$$ - If $p < 1/4$: then $2p - 1/2 < 0$. Choosing any $\delta > 0$ strictly reduces expected cost! (e.g. For $p = 1/6$ in A3 Q1e, $2(1/6) - 1/2 = -1/6 < 0$, yielding profit $\delta/6$). Thus, $f_p$ is NOT strategyproof for any $p < 1/4$. - If $p \ge 1/4$: then $2p - 1/2 \ge 0$, so $\delta(2p - 1/2) \ge 0$. Outward deviation never strictly reduces expected cost.

Step 3: Analysis of Inward Deviation ($x_1' = x_1 + \delta$ with $0 < \delta < d$)
If Agent 1 reports inward $x_1' = x_1 + \delta$: - At $x_1'$: distance is $\delta$. - At $x_2$: distance is $d$. - At midpoint: distance is $\frac{d + \delta}{2}$. $$\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}_1] = p\delta + pd + (1 - 2p)\frac{d + \delta}{2} = \frac{d}{2} + \delta \left( p + \frac{1 - 2p}{2} \right) = \frac{d}{2} + \frac{\delta}{2} > \frac{d}{2}$$ Inward deviation strictly increases expected cost for all $p$.
Reporting past Agent 2 ($x_1' > x_2$) places the facility even further right, giving strictly greater cost.
By symmetry, the exact same analysis holds for Agent 2.
Therefore, $f_p$ is strategyproof in expectation if and only if $p \ge 1/4$. $\blacksquare$

Part (b): Approximation Ratio and Optimality of $p = 1/4$

The optimal maximum cost is achieved at the midpoint $\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$, where optimal maximum cost is $\text{OPT} = \frac{d}{2}$.
Under mechanism $f_p$: - With probability $p$, facility is at $x_1$: maximum cost is $|x_1 - x_2| = d$. - With probability $p$, facility is at $x_2$: maximum cost is $|x_2 - x_1| = d$. - With probability $1 - 2p$, facility is at midpoint: maximum cost is $\frac{d}{2}$. The expected maximum cost is: $$\mathbb{E}[\text{MaxCost}(f_p)] = p(d) + p(d) + (1 - 2p)\frac{d}{2} = 2pd + \frac{d}{2} - pd = \left( p + \frac{1}{2} \right) d$$ The approximation ratio is: $$\text{Ratio}(p) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\text{MaxCost}(f_p)]}{\text{OPT}} = \frac{\left( p + \frac{1}{2} \right) d}{\frac{d}{2}} = 2p + 1$$ Notice that $\text{Ratio}(p) = 2p + 1$ is strictly increasing in $p$ on $[1/4, 1/2]$: - At $p = 1/4$: $\text{Ratio}(1/4) = 2(1/4) + 1 = \frac{3}{2}$. - At $p = 1/2$ (Random Dictatorship): $\text{Ratio}(1/2) = 2(1/2) + 1 = 2$. Since $p \ge 1/4$ is required for strategyproofness, the minimum possible approximation ratio among all strategyproof mechanisms in this family is achieved uniquely at $p = 1/4$, yielding the optimal ratio of $3/2$. $\blacksquare$
questions.reference: Part (a): Truthful expected cost is d/2. Outward deviation x1' = x1 - delta gives E[cost] = d/2 + delta(2p - 1/2). If p < 1/4, 2p - 1/2 < 0 so outward misreport strictly profits. If p >= 1/4, outward gives delta(2p - 1/2) >= 0 and inward gives delta/2 > 0, so no deviation profits. Part (b): E[MaxCost] = (p + 1/2)d, while OPT = d/2. Ratio(p) = 2p + 1. Strictly increasing in p, so minimum over strategyproof range [1/4, 1/2] is at p = 1/4, giving ratio 3/2.
rubric: 2 marks: Formally evaluates truthful expected cost d/2 and shows it is independent of p
2 marks: Derives the outward deviation formula d/2 + delta(2p - 1/2) and proves p < 1/4 is strictly manipulable
1 mark: Shows inward deviation costs d/2 + delta/2 > d/2, establishing strategyproofness iff p >= 1/4
2 marks: Derives expected maximum cost (p + 1/2)d and approximation ratio Ratio(p) = 2p + 1
1 mark: Concludes p = 1/4 uniquely minimizes Ratio(p) over [1/4, 1/2] to achieve 3/2

questions.topic: Convergence of Asynchronous BR Dynamics vs. Simultaneous Cycling in Congestion Games
questions.prompt: Consider an unweighted atomic congestion game $\Gamma = (N, E, (S_i)_{i \in N}, (c_e)_{e \in E})$ with finite players $N$ and non-decreasing latency functions $c_e: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. (a) (5 Marks) Asynchronous Best-Response Dynamics (Cycle Impossibility): Suppose the game is played dynamically: at each step $t \ge 0$, if strategy profile $s^t$ is not a Nash equilibrium, an arbitrary single player $i$ with a profitable deviation unilaterally switches to a strictly better strategy $s_i^{t+1}$ such that $C_i(s_i^{t+1}, s_{-i}^t) < C_i(s_i^t, s_{-i}^t)$, while all other players remain fixed ($s_{-i}^{t+1} = s_{-i}^t$). Prove using Rosenthal's potential function $\Phi(s) = \sum_{e \in E} \sum_{k=1}^{f_e(s)} c_e(k)$ that this asynchronous process can never cycle, and must terminate at a pure Nash equilibrium in a finite number of steps. (b) (3 Marks) Simultaneous Best-Response Dynamics (Infinite Cycling Counterexample): Now suppose players update simultaneously: at each step $t$, all players with a profitable deviation simultaneously switch to their best response against $s^t$. Prove that simultaneous best-response dynamics can cycle indefinitely without ever converging to a Nash equilibrium. Construct an explicit 2-player, 2-edge congestion game, identify the pure Nash equilibrium, and demonstrate an initial state that enters a permanent 2-cycle $(s^0 \leftrightarrow s^1)$.
questions.blueprint:
Proof Blueprint (Exact Assignment Style)

Part (a): Asynchronous Best-Response Dynamics & Cycle Impossibility

Step 1: Rosenthal's Potential as a Strict Lyapunov Function
Recall Rosenthal's potential function for strategy profile $s \in S = \prod_{j=1}^n S_j$: $$\Phi(s) = \sum_{e \in E} \sum_{k=1}^{f_e(s)} c_e(k)$$ By the exact potential property (as proved in Paper 2 Question 6), for any single player $i$ unilaterally switching from $s_i^t$ to $s_i^{t+1}$: $$\Phi(s^{t+1}) - \Phi(s^t) = C_i(s_i^{t+1}, s_{-i}^t) - C_i(s_i^t, s_{-i}^t)$$

Step 2: Strict Monotonicity Along Unilateral Improvement Paths
In asynchronous dynamics, player $i$ moves if and only if the deviation is strictly profitable: $$C_i(s_i^{t+1}, s_{-i}^t) < C_i(s_i^t, s_{-i}^t) \iff C_i(s_i^{t+1}, s_{-i}^t) - C_i(s_i^t, s_{-i}^t) < 0$$ Applying the exact potential identity: $$\Phi(s^{t+1}) - \Phi(s^t) < 0 \iff \Phi(s^{t+1}) < \Phi(s^t)$$ Thus, the potential function $\Phi$ strictly decreases at EVERY single step of the dynamics: $$\Phi(s^0) > \Phi(s^1) > \Phi(s^2) > \dots$$

Step 3: Impossibility of Cycles and Finite Termination
1. Cycle Impossibility: Suppose for contradiction that the sequence of states enters a cycle: $$s^{t} \to s^{t+1} \to \dots \to s^{t+K} = s^t \quad (K \ge 1)$$ Then by strict monotonicity: $$\Phi(s^t) > \Phi(s^{t+1}) > \dots > \Phi(s^{t+K}) = \Phi(s^t)$$ $$\implies \Phi(s^t) > \Phi(s^t)$$ which is a direct contradiction! Hence, no state can ever be visited more than once, and cycles are impossible.
2. Finite Termination: The strategy profile space $S = \prod_{i=1}^n S_i$ is a finite set because each player has a finite number of available paths. Since $S$ is finite, there are at most $|S| < \infty$ distinct strategy profiles. Since each step visits a strictly new profile, the process cannot continue indefinitely. It must terminate after at most $|S|$ steps.
3. Equilibrium at Termination: The process terminates only when NO player has a strictly profitable unilateral deviation. By definition, a strategy profile where no player has a profitable unilateral deviation is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. $\blacksquare$

Part (b): Simultaneous Best-Response Dynamics & Infinite Cycling

Game Construction:
Consider $n = 2$ players routing 1 unit each between $s$ and $t$ across two parallel edges $E = \{e_1, e_2\}$. Let the latency functions be: $$c_1(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x = 1 \\ 10 & \text{if } x = 2 \end{cases}, \qquad c_2(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x = 1 \\ 10 & \text{if } x = 2 \end{cases}$$ (Both functions are strictly non-decreasing). Strategy sets: $S_1 = S_2 = \{e_1, e_2\}$.

Pure Nash Equilibria:
The profiles $(e_1, e_2)$ and $(e_2, e_1)$ are pure Nash equilibria: each player experiences latency $1$, and unilaterally switching would induce load $x = 2$ on the other edge, giving latency $10 > 1$. Neither player wants to deviate.

Demonstrating the Infinite 2-Cycle:
Start at initial profile $s^0 = (e_1, e_1)$ (both players on edge 1): - Current latency for both players is $c_1(2) = 10$. - Player 1 evaluates switching to $e_2$: she would face load $1$ on $e_2$, experiencing latency $c_2(1) = 1 < 10$. Hence, $e_2$ is Player 1's unique best response. - Player 2 symmetrically evaluates switching to $e_2$: she would face load $1$ on $e_2$, experiencing latency $c_2(1) = 1 < 10$. Hence, $e_2$ is Player 2's unique best response. Under simultaneous updating, BOTH players switch to $e_2$ at the exact same instant!

The resulting state at $t = 1$ is: $$s^1 = (e_2, e_2)$$ At state $s^1 = (e_2, e_2)$: - Current latency for both players is $c_2(2) = 10$. - Player 1 evaluates switching to $e_1$: latency would be $c_1(1) = 1 < 10$. Best response is $e_1$. - Player 2 evaluates switching to $e_1$: latency would be $c_1(1) = 1 < 10$. Best response is $e_1$. Under simultaneous updating, BOTH players switch back to $e_1$!

The resulting state at $t = 2$ is: $$s^2 = (e_1, e_1) = s^0$$ The dynamics enter a permanent, infinite 2-cycle: $$(e_1, e_1) \longleftrightarrow (e_2, e_2)$$ never reaching either pure Nash equilibrium $(e_1, e_2)$ or $(e_2, e_1)$! $\blacksquare$
questions.reference: Part (a): Potential property gives Phi(s^{t+1}) - Phi(s^t) = C_i(s_i^{t+1}, s_{-i}^t) - C_i(s_i^t, s_{-i}^t) < 0. Phi strictly decreases at every step. In a cycle, Phi(s^t) > Phi(s^t), contradiction. Since S is finite, sequence must terminate at a state with no profitable deviations, which is a pure NE. Part (b): 2 players on parallel edges e1, e2 with c(1)=1, c(2)=10. At (e1, e1) both pay 10 and best-respond to e2. Simultaneous move yields (e2, e2). At (e2, e2) both pay 10 and best-respond to e1. Simultaneous move yields (e1, e1). Indefinite 2-cycle, never reaching pure NE (e1, e2).
rubric: 2 marks: Formulates exact potential identity Phi(s^{t+1}) - Phi(s^t) = Delta C_i < 0 for asynchronous moves
2 marks: Uses strict monotonicity to prove cycle impossibility by contradiction (Phi(s) > Phi(s))
1 mark: Invokes finiteness of strategy space S to establish finite termination at a pure Nash equilibrium
2 marks: Constructs valid 2-player 2-edge congestion game and defines non-decreasing latencies (e.g. c(1)=1, c(2)=10)
1 mark: Explicitly verifies the permanent 2-cycle (e1, e1) <-> (e2, e2) under simultaneous updates

questions.solution:
(a) Without player 2, 3, or 4, the remaining total weight is below 9. Without player 1 it is exactly 9. Thus 2, 3, and 4 are veto players.

(b) The winning coalition $\{2,3,4\}$ needs payoff at least 1. Efficiency and nonnegativity force $x_1=0$ and $x_2+x_3+x_4=1$. These conditions are also sufficient.

questions.topic: Proof: Round-Robin Produces an EF1 Allocation

sources.title: Week 8 lecture · Fair allocation of indivisible goods

questions.prompt: There are $n$ agents with additive, nonnegative valuations. In a fixed cyclic order $1,2,\ldots,n$, each agent picks a remaining good of maximum value to herself, until no goods remain. Prove that the final allocation is EF1. Handle both relative orders of an arbitrary pair of agents and an incomplete final round.
questions.blueprint:
Worked proof

1. Fix a pair and label picks
Fix distinct agents i,j. Let $a_t$ be i's t-th pick and $b_t$ j's t-th pick. Compare bundles using $v_i$, not $v_j$. Nonnegativity lets us ignore unmatched extra goods in i's bundle.

2. When i picks before j
Whenever $b_t$ exists, $a_t$ exists and i chose while $b_t$ was still available. Thus $v_i(a_t)\ge v_i(b_t)$. Summing shows $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j)$, even if i has an extra pick in the last round.

3. When j picks before i
Remove j's first pick $b_1$. Whenever $b_{t+1}$ exists, $a_t$ exists and i chose it before j picked $b_{t+1}$. Therefore $v_i(a_t)\ge v_i(b_{t+1})$. Summing gives $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{b_1\})$. This also handles an incomplete last round.

4. Conclude EF1
For each ordered pair, either i has no envy or removing j's first good eliminates it. Empty bundles cause no envy under nonnegative valuations. Hence for every nonempty $A_j$ there exists a good g with $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$, which is EF1.
rubric: 2 marks: Fixes an arbitrary pair and uses the observer’s additive valuation.
2 marks: Pairs same-round picks when i precedes j.
3 marks: Pairs i’s t-th pick with j’s (t+1)-th pick and removes j’s first good.
1 mark: Handles the incomplete round and empty bundles, then concludes EF1.
questions.reference: Compare using vi. If i precedes j, pair same-round picks. If j precedes i, remove j’s first good and pair a_t with b_(t+1). Additivity and nonnegativity yield EF1, including an incomplete final round.

questions.solution:
(a) The only varying inclusions require $3\le c\le7$.

(b,c) Efficiency gives $x_1+x_2+x_3=7$. From $x_1+x_3\ge5$ we get $x_2\le2$, while individual rationality requires $x_2\ge2$. Thus $x_2=2$. Next $x_1+x_2\ge4$ gives $x_1\ge2$, and $x_3\ge3$ gives $x_1\le2$. Therefore every core vector must be $(2,2,3)$. It satisfies the remaining coalition inequality exactly when $c\le5$. Combining with monotonicity gives $c\in[3,5]$.

(d) Average marginal contributions over six permutations: $\phi_1=(10-c)/3$, $\phi_2=(8+c)/6$, $\phi_3=(14+c)/6$. At c=5 this is $(5/3,13/6,19/6)$. This Shapley vector is not in the core: coalition $\{1,2\}$ receives $23/6<4$. A nonempty core does not guarantee Shapley membership.
questions.reference: Monotone for c in [3,7]. Monotone singleton core for c in [3,5], vector (2,2,3). At c=5 Shapley=(5/3,13/6,19/6), blocked by {1,2}.

questions.topic: Round-Robin, Maximin Shares, and Fairness Checks

sources.title: Week 8 lecture · Fair allocation of indivisible goods

questions.prompt:
There are three agents and four goods. Values are additive and nonnegative:

$$\begin{array}{c|rrrr}&g_1&g_2&g_3&g_4\\\hline1&11&10&5&1\\2&1&6&1&2\\3&8&7&4&9\end{array}$$

subparts.label: (a)
subparts.prompt: Compute the maximin shares (MMS1,MMS2,MMS3) for a partition into three bundles.

subparts.label: (b)
subparts.prompt: Run round-robin in order 1,2,3. Enter the final bundles (A1; A2; A3).

subparts.label: (c)
subparts.prompt: Compute the agents’ own utilities (v1(A1),v2(A2),v3(A3)).

subparts.label: (d)
subparts.prompt: Is the result envy-free? Is it EFX? Enter (Yes/No, Yes/No) in that order.

questions.solution:
(a) Partitions attaining the shares are $\{g_1\},\{g_2\},\{g_3,g_4\}$ for agent 1 (minimum 6), $\{g_1,g_3\},\{g_2\},\{g_4\}$ for agent 2 (minimum 2), and $\{g_1\},\{g_2,g_3\},\{g_4\}$ for agent 3 (minimum 8). With four goods and three nonempty bundles, at least two bundles are singletons. Exceeding 6, 2, or 8, respectively, would force two singleton bundles that leave too little value for the third; these shares are optimal.

(b,c) The picks are $g_1,g_2,g_4,g_3$, giving $A_1=\{g_1,g_3\}$, $A_2=\{g_2\}$, $A_3=\{g_4\}$ and utilities $(16,6,9)$.

(d) Agent 3 values agent 1's bundle at $8+4=12>9$, so the result is not envy-free. Removing either good from that bundle leaves value 4 or 8, at most 9. The other agents have no envy. Thus it is EFX (and hence EF1). This particular round-robin output is EFX; round-robin does not guarantee EFX in general.
questions.reference: MMS=(6,2,8); bundles {g1,g3};{g2};{g4}; own utilities (16,6,9); not envy-free but EFX.

questions.topic: Comparing Utilitarian, Egalitarian, and Nash Welfare

sources.title: Week 7 lecture · Stable matching and bargaining

questions.prompt: Utilities are $u_1=x$, $u_2=y$. The feasible set is $x,y\ge0$ and $x+2y\le12$, with disagreement utilities $(0,0)$.

subparts.label: (a)
subparts.prompt: Find the utilitarian optimum (x,y).

subparts.label: (b)
subparts.prompt: Find the egalitarian optimum maximizing min(x,y).

subparts.label: (c)
subparts.prompt: Find the Nash-product optimum (x,y).

questions.solution:
(a) On the frontier, $y=(12-x)/2$ and $x+y=6+x/2$, maximized at $(12,0)$.

(b) To achieve a minimum utility t, both utilities must be at least t, requiring $3t\le12$. The upper bound t=4 is attained uniquely at $(4,4)$.

(c) The product is $x(12-x)/2$, with derivative $6-x$. Its maximum is at x=6,y=3 with product 18; the endpoints have product zero. All three optima lie on the Pareto frontier but differ because their objectives differ.
questions.reference: Utilitarian (12,0); egalitarian (4,4); Nash-product (6,3).

questions.topic: Stable Matching: Comparing the Two Proposing Sides

sources.title: Week 7 lecture · Stable matching and bargaining

questions.prompt:
Students: $A:X\succ Y\succ Z$, $B:Y\succ X\succ Z$, $C:X\succ Y\succ Z$.

Hospitals: $X:B\succ A\succ C$, $Y:A\succ B\succ C$, $Z:C\succ A\succ B$.

All lists are strict and complete; each hospital has one place.

subparts.label: (a)
subparts.prompt: Run student-proposing Gale–Shapley. Enter A,B,C’s hospitals.

subparts.label: (b)
subparts.prompt: Run hospital-proposing Gale–Shapley. Enter A,B,C’s hospitals.

subparts.label: (c)
subparts.prompt: How many stable matchings exist for this instance?

questions.solution:
(a) A proposes to X, B to Y, and C to X. X keeps A; C is rejected by X then Y and finally accepted by Z. The result is $(A,X),(B,Y),(C,Z)$.

(b) X proposes to B, Y to A, and Z to C. Each is accepted immediately: $(A,Y),(B,X),(C,Z)$.

(c) C must be assigned to Z in any stable matching. Otherwise whichever of A or B is at Z blocks with C's hospital: that student prefers X or Y to Z and both X and Y prefer A and B to C. The two possible assignments of A,B to X,Y are both stable. Therefore exactly two stable matchings exist.
questions.reference: Student-proposing (X,Y,Z); hospital-proposing (Y,X,Z); exactly 2 stable matchings, with C assigned to Z in both.

questions.prompt: Answer Yes or No for general transferable-utility cooperative games.

subparts.prompt: If a game’s core contains two distinct payoff vectors, must it contain infinitely many payoff vectors?
subparts.explanation: The core is an intersection of linear constraints, hence convex. Every convex combination of the two distinct vectors is in the core, giving a line segment with infinitely many points.

subparts.label: (b)
subparts.prompt: If a game has a nonempty core, must its Shapley vector belong to the core?

questions.solution: Convexity of the core as a set follows from linear inequalities, even when the cooperative game is not a convex game. A fair marginal-contribution rule need not satisfy every coalition's stability constraint.

questions.topic: Proof: A Common Hospital Ranking Gives a Unique Stable Matching

sources.title: Week 7 lecture · Stable matching and bargaining

questions.prompt: There are n students and n hospitals, each with one place. All preferences are strict and complete. Every hospital ranks the students in the same order $s_1\succ s_2\succ\cdots\succ s_n$. Prove that a unique stable matching exists. Describe how to construct it.
questions.blueprint:
Worked proof

1. Construct the candidate
Process students in the common ranking order. Give $s_1$ her favorite hospital, then $s_2$ her favorite remaining hospital, and so on. Strict preferences make every choice unique.

2. Show each assignment is forced
In any stable matching, $s_1$ must receive her favorite hospital h. Otherwise she prefers h to her assignment, and h prefers her to its assigned student, a blocking pair. After fixing $s_1$, apply the same argument to $s_2$ and her favorite remaining hospital. Inductively, each assignment is forced.

3. Establish stability
Consider a pair $s_i,h$ where $s_i$ prefers h to her constructed assignment. Hospital h was unavailable at her turn, so it is assigned to some $s_j$ with j

4. Conclude existence and uniqueness
The constructed matching has no blocking pair, so it is stable. Every stable matching has all its assignments forced to equal this construction, so there is exactly one.
rubric: 2 marks: Gives the common-ranking serial construction with unique choices.
3 marks: Forces the top student’s assignment and extends the argument inductively.
2 marks: Shows a desired but unavailable hospital prefers its earlier-ranked assigned student.
1 mark: Concludes both existence and uniqueness under the stated assumptions.
questions.reference: Assign students in the common hospital order to their favorite remaining hospitals. Every assignment is forced by a potential blocking pair. The construction is stable because unavailable preferred hospitals have higher-ranked students, hence the stable matching is unique.

questions.topic: Assignment 8: Welfare, Pareto Improvements, and MMS

sources.title: Week 8 lecture · Fair allocation of indivisible goods

questions.prompt:
Three agents have additive, nonnegative valuations:

$$\begin{array}{c|rrrr}&g_1&g_2&g_3&g_4\\\hline1&40&30&20&10\\2&0&40&30&30\\3&30&0&20&50\end{array}$$

The specified allocation is $A_1=\{g_1\}$, $A_2=\{g_4\}$, and $A_3=\{g_2,g_3\}$.

subparts.label: (a)
subparts.prompt: What is the maximum utilitarian welfare over all allocations?

subparts.label: (b)
subparts.prompt: What is the maximum egalitarian welfare over all allocations?

subparts.label: (c)
subparts.prompt: Compute the maximin shares (MMS1,MMS2,MMS3).

subparts.label: (d)
subparts.prompt: For the specified allocation A, do all agents receive at least their MMS? Is A Pareto optimal? Enter (Yes/No, Yes/No) in that order.

questions.solution:
(a) Give each good to an agent with maximum value: $g_1$ to 1, $g_2,g_3$ to 2, and $g_4$ to 3. The sum is $40+40+30+50=160$.

(b) Give $g_1$ to 1, $g_2$ to 2, and $g_3,g_4$ to 3. Utilities are $(40,40,70)$, so minimum welfare 40 is attainable. A minimum above 40 would require all three agents to exceed 40. Four goods split among three nonempty bundles leave at least two singleton bundles, but only $g_4$ has a value above 40 for any agent. This is impossible, so 40 is optimal.

(c) Agent 1 can partition into $\{g_1\},\{g_2\},\{g_3,g_4\}$ with minimum 30. Agent 2 can use $\{g_2\},\{g_3\},\{g_1,g_4\}$, also minimum 30. Agent 3 can use $\{g_1\},\{g_3\},\{g_2,g_4\}$ with minimum 20. For agent 1, a minimum above 30 would require at least two singleton goods above 30, but only $g_1$ qualifies. For agent 2 only $g_2$ exceeds 30. For agent 3 only $g_1,g_4$ exceed 20, leaving a bundle of value 20. Hence the MMS vector is $(30,30,20)$.

(d) The specified allocation gives $(40,30,20)$, meeting every MMS. It is not Pareto optimal: $B_1=\{g_1\}$, $B_2=\{g_2\}$, $B_3=\{g_3,g_4\}$ gives $(40,40,70)$, improving agents 2 and 3 without hurting agent 1. MMS satisfaction alone does not imply Pareto optimality.
questions.reference: Maximum utilitarian welfare 160; maximum egalitarian welfare 40; MMS=(30,30,20). A gives (40,30,20), so it is MMS but not Pareto optimal; allocation {g1};{g2};{g3,g4} Pareto dominates it.

questions.topic: Proof: An Existing MMS Allocation Can Be Pareto Optimal

sources.title: Week 8 lecture · Fair allocation of indivisible goods

questions.prompt: There are finitely many agents and indivisible goods, with additive nonnegative valuations. Suppose at least one complete allocation gives every agent at least her maximin share. Prove that there exists a complete allocation that is both MMS and Pareto optimal among all complete allocations. Do not assume that every instance has an MMS allocation.
questions.blueprint:
Worked proof

1. Define the feasible MMS set.
Let $\mathcal M$ be the set of complete allocations A with $v_i(A_i)\ge\mathrm{MMS}_i$ for all i. By assumption this set is nonempty. It is finite because there are at most $n^m$ complete assignments of m goods to n agents.

2. Choose a welfare maximizer within that set.
Choose $A^*\in\arg\max_{A\in\mathcal M}\sum_i v_i(A_i)$. A maximizer exists because $\mathcal M$ is finite and nonempty.

3. Any Pareto improvement stays MMS.
Suppose a complete allocation B Pareto dominates $A^*$. Then $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i^*)\ge\mathrm{MMS}_i$ for every i, so $B\in\mathcal M$.

4. Derive the contradiction.
At least one agent strictly improves and none is worse, so $\sum_i v_i(B_i)>\sum_i v_i(A_i^*)$, contradicting maximality within $\mathcal M$. Thus no complete allocation Pareto dominates $A^*$, which is both MMS and Pareto optimal. The argument is conditional on an MMS allocation existing.
rubric: 2 marks: Defines a finite, nonempty set of MMS allocations using the assumption.
2 marks: Selects an allocation maximizing the sum of utilities within that set.
2 marks: Shows that any Pareto-dominating allocation still satisfies every MMS bound.
2 marks: Uses strict welfare improvement to contradict maximality and concludes Pareto optimality.
questions.reference: Among the finite nonempty set of MMS allocations, maximize total utility. Any Pareto improvement also meets every MMS bound and strictly raises total utility, a contradiction. Thus the chosen allocation is Pareto optimal and MMS.

questions.prompt: Strong EF1 (s-EF1) requires that for every nonempty bundle $A_j$, there exists one good $g_j\in A_j$ such that $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g_j\})$ for every other agent i. Assume additive nonnegative valuations.

subparts.label: (a)
subparts.prompt: How does the quantifier order differ from ordinary EF1?
options: Ordinary EF1 requires every good to remove all envy.
Ordinary EF1 and s-EF1 have identical quantifiers.
Strong EF1 requires one good per envied bundle that works for every observer; ordinary EF1 may use a different good for each observer.
Strong EF1 requires a different good for every observer, while ordinary EF1 requires the same one.
subparts.explanation: Ordinary EF1 says for every ordered pair $(i,j)$ there exists a suitable good. Strong EF1 says for each j there exists a good that works for all i. Moving the existential quantifier before the observer's universal quantifier makes the requirement stronger.

subparts.label: (b)
subparts.prompt: Is a fixed-order round-robin allocation always s-EF1? If so, which good can be removed from each nonempty bundle?
options: No; round-robin guarantees only ordinary EF1.
Yes; remove the first good that the owner picked.
Yes; remove the last good that the owner picked.
Yes; remove any good, since round-robin always guarantees EFX.
subparts.explanation: Fix owner j and remove her first pick. Agents earlier in the round-robin order do not envy j even before removal. For any later agent i, i's t-th pick was chosen before j's (t+1)-th pick, so $v_i(a_t)\ge v_i(b_{t+1})$. Summing gives the required inequality for every observer using the same first good. Nonnegativity handles unmatched goods and empty bundles.

questions.solution: Strong EF1 asks for a common witness good for each bundle. In round-robin, the owner's first pick is a common witness: earlier agents have no envy, and later agents can compare their picks to the owner's picks starting at the second. This strengthens the usual round-robin EF1 proof.
questions.reference: s-EF1 uses one removable good per owner that works for every observer. Fixed cyclic round-robin is s-EF1: remove the owner’s first pick.
